cases.note: The value of an invocation nobody has made. Every default is "not gathered", and nothing about it advances — the same opening assertion §27's machine has, for the same reason.
An invocation arrived. §54.1: a skill is invoked with arguments and terminates, which is the whole distinction from a policy.

The case that matters most in this file. A runtime that has not evaluated §54.2 yet must not be able to start a skill by failing to ask, so `null` holds the machine where it is rather than letting it through. "Not assume true, which is what free-text preconditions do by construction."
cases.expected: {"changed":false,"detail":"the entry predicates have not been evaluated, and an unevaluated precondition is not a satisfied one","from":"preconditions","outcome":null,"reason":"preconditions_pending","release_leases":false,"to":"preconditions"}

cases.note: §54.6's `skill.preconditions.enforced`: refused, with the predicate named. The naming is shared between two functions — `evaluatePreconditions` finds the clause and the lifecycle carries it into what an operator reads — and neither is complete alone.
And a refusal with no clause to name still refuses. A caller that lost the report must not be able to turn a refusal into a start.
On to §25.2.

§54.5: "leases are held by the root invocation, not re-acquired per call. Nested acquisition is how you get a skill deadlocking against its own child." The one composition limit that is not a graph property, and it lives here.
cases.expected: {"changed":true,"detail":"a nested call runs under the root invocation's leases (§54.5)","from":"preconditions","outcome":null,"reason":"leases_held_by_root","release_leases":false,"to":"running"}

cases.note: A lease nobody has taken is not one that was granted — the same rule as the precondition above, arrived at from §25.2 rather than from §54.2.

§25.2 refuses rather than interleaves: "two policies alternating commands to the same joint produce a trajectory neither was trained on and neither can be held responsible for." The token and the holder reach the detail, because an operator has to know which package to stop.

The other half of §25.2, and the one no case had. A token the operator never granted reports no holder — "nobody has the arm, this package may not ask for it" — and the refusal has to say that rather than "held by another package", which sends an operator hunting for a package that does not exist when the fix is one grant. Found by writing a runtime, not by reading the document.
cases.expected: {"changed":true,"detail":"`manipulation.grasp` was never granted to this package, so §25.2 will not let it take the lease — nobody is holding it. Grant it, or take it out of `required_capabilities`.","from":"acquiring","outcome":"aborted","reason":"lease_denied","release_leases":true,"to":"terminal"}

cases.note: And a denial that names no token at all says so, rather than blaming a package. This is the shape a caller produces by forgetting a field, and inventing a holder for it would be the same lie in a quieter place.
cases.expected: {"changed":true,"detail":"a required capability could not be leased, and nothing named which","from":"acquiring","outcome":"aborted","reason":"lease_denied","release_leases":true,"to":"terminal"}

Still running is a fixed point, which is what makes this safe to call every cycle from a loop that runs faster than the work.
§54.6's `skill.timeout.enforced`. A 10 s estimate at the default factor of 2 is 20 000 ms, and the comparison is inclusive: a skill that has used exactly its budget has used it.
cases.expected: {"changed":true,"detail":"past 20000 ms, which is the declared estimate times 2","from":"running","outcome":"aborted","reason":"timeout","release_leases":true,"to":"terminal"}

cases.note: One millisecond the other side of it.

A skill that declares no duration produces an unenforceable deadline, and `skillDeadline` deliberately does not decide whether such a skill may run. Neither does this: what it does not do is invent a ceiling.
§54.6's `skill.preconditions.rechecked`. §54.2: "battery dropping below reserve mid-skill should stop the skill, not be discovered at the end."

cases.note: The exclusion worth pinning. `hold` is where §27's machine sits between a lease being granted and a policy actually commanding, so aborting on it would kill every skill in the moment it started. A guard asking for a hold arrives as `guard_tripped` instead.
§27's `DEGRADED` row runs. §45.5 makes an unavailable guard the ordinary case, and a skill refusing to proceed on one would refuse on most real robots.

Every abort condition at once. A timeout makes the OS stop the skill under a controlled stop and a guard trip stops the robot, so both *produce* a robot that is no longer commanding — and reporting the robot state here would hide the cause behind its own consequence. Timeout wins.

cases.note: A skill already terminal releases nothing. A release emitted every cycle after a skill ended would be a release racing the next invocation's acquisition, which is the one way §25.2's arbitration can be lost by the thing that implements it.
